Artificial Intelligence in English Language
Teaching in Thailand: Conflicting Results and
Methodological Limitations

                                   Introduction

        Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly changing the world, and English
language teaching (ELT) is no exception. In recent years, interest in using and
researching Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools to boost the effectiveness of
English Language Teaching and Learning has been remarkably growing both
globally and locally such as Thailand. In Thailand, a great number of studies
on the use of AI in English language teaching has been published (e.g.
Apridayani et al., 2025; Boontong et al., 2025; Chumpavan et al., 2024;
Songsiengchai, 2025; Tanharat & Phootirat, 2025; Thongsan & Anderson,
2025; Waluyo & Kusumastuti, 2024). These studies reveal critical issues
concerning the conflicting results of the use of AI in terms of learner
outcomes, learners’ attitudes towards AI, research contexts and research
methodologies. This raises the need to synthesize and analyze the literature
on the use of AI in teaching and learning English as a global language in Thai
educational contexts.
        This study is an initial attempt to synthesize the empirical findings of
these studies to uncover the controversies and knowledge gaps regarding the
use of AI in teaching and learning English in the current educational
landscape of Thailand. The aim of the paper is to call for collaborative
scholarly efforts to address these context-specific tensions so that AI tools
can be utilized with sound pedagogies.

          The literature included in this critical analysis was identified through
searches across major academic databases and scholarly indices using
keywords related to AI applications in language learning, with a specific focus
on the Thai higher education context. The articles were selected based on
their relevance to key themes, including learner outcomes, pedagogical
challenges, and methodological approaches. This selection prioritized recent
empirical research published within the last five years to highlight current
controversies and knowledge gaps.
          The paper begins with a brief discussion of how AI has influenced
ELT, what benefits it offers, and what challenges are emerging on the global
scale. This is followed by a review of the most recent literature on the use of
AI in ELT in Thailand. The paper concludes with recommendations on
critical issues that need further research to inform the future use of AI tools
in ELT in Thai educational ecology.

      The Global Use of AI tools in ELT: Benefits and Challenges

        Artificial Intelligence (AI) has developed from rule-based AI, which
was designed for administrative efficiency and corrective feedback to
Generative AI (GenAI) and Large Language Models (LLMs) and has become
increasingly integral to educational systems in almost every country. This has
shifted the pedagogical paradigm from computer-assisted instruction to AI-
driven cognitive partnership. It has been recognized that educational
technologies. The integration of AI into educational settings marks a
transformative shift, offering unprecedented opportunities to personalize
learning, enhance student engagement, and optimize educational outcomes
(Zheng et al., 2021).
        The benefits of GenAI to ELT teachers and learners are numerous
and the potential is bound to increase as technology is still fast developing.
AI has supported language teaching and learning with studies in different
aspects for both learners and teachers. For learners, personalized and
immediate feedback are valuable for second or third language learners who
need consistent correction and practice. AI addresses this need by creating
adaptive learning environments, and efficiently providing feedback,
identifying learners’ strengths and weaknesses, and developing their language
skills more effectively (Luckin & Cukurova, 2019; Mepo & Rigia, 2025). It has
been observed that AI applications in ELT also help overcome challenges in
developing the four core language skills: speaking, reading, writing, and
listening. Learners use AI-powered platforms to practice these skills in a
supportive environment, which research indicates improves their self-
regulated learning and confidence. Additionally, conversational AI tools help
develop learners' emotional and cognitive skills, enriching the language

learning experience by creating interactive and engaging practice
opportunities (Lai & Lee, 2024).
         On the side of teachers, AI can be of help by reducing workload
through automated feedback, error correction, and lesson planning. This is
especially useful in large classrooms where giving timely and consistent
personalized feedback can be challenging. AI tools allow teachers to give
instant, detailed feedback on language tasks, thereby meeting the need for
individualized support (Mepo & Rigia, 2025; Pokrivčáková, 2019; Syafei &
Nuraeningsih, 2025). Furthermore, AI can act as a support system, providing
tailored assistance that adjusts to each learner's progress, instilling more
independent and effective language learning habits. As the use of AI in
language education has been increasingly widespread, this article aims to
examine empirical findings and explore how AI is being applied in the Thai
ELT context.
         Despite the potential of AI to support language education such as
offering new tools and resources to enhance learning, their use also raises
important questions regarding ethics and responsibility (Cogo et al., 2024).
While studies reveal the benefits of AI-enhanced English language learning,
researchers also report relevant concerns such as incidences of academic
dishonesty or students’ attempts to take advantages of AI tools to gain unfair
advantages (Xie et al., 2023). Kohnke et al. (2023) reported the results of a
qualitative study on a small group of Hong Kong University instructors
(N=12) that teachers lacked digital competencies and pedagogical knowledge
needed to effectively implement AI tools in the classroom.

                        AI Application in ELT Context

        In the AI era, understanding how AI works and impacts people’s lives
has become a growing priority in both educational and research contexts.
There has been an increasing number of studies regarding AI applications by
English language learners and educators since AI has gained tremendous
popularity among scholars worldwide. Empirical research consistently shows
that AI-driven tools, such as chatbots and automated writing tools, enhance
learners’ language skills, particularly in writing, reading, speaking, and
vocabulary development (Ekizer, 2025; Lai & Lee, 2024; Mepo & Rigia,
2025). For instance, Grammarly, Chat GPT, and You.com serve as an
assistant writing tool that provides real-time feedback on grammar,
vocabulary, and structure (Giray, 2024; Özdere, 2025), leading to improved
accuracy, broadened lexical repertoire, and learner confidence (Syafei &
Nuraeningsih, 2025).
        Additionally, ELSA Speak, Replica, Duolingo, and Orai AI are AI-
powered language learning applications EFL learners use to practice their

speaking skills (Alpika, 2026; Kristiawan et. al., 2024; Tolstykh &
Oshchepkova, 2024; Tuong & Dan, 2024; Warman et al., 2023). Moreover,
Google’s Speech-to-Text API and AI Speak provide feedback on fluency,
intonation, rhythm, pitch, and phonetics developing learners’ awareness in
improving verbal skills (Dennis, 2024; Liakina & Liakin, 2023).
          Research shows that learners, especially the struggling readers,
remarkably develop their reading comprehension when they use Chatbots
and Conversational AI tools (Silor & Silor, 2025). Kusumawati et al. (2025)
also observed that TuinLec, and AI-integrated Intelligent tutoring systems
(ITS) served as a scaffold in enhancing elementary students’ abilities to
identify main ideas and interpreting the organization of texts. Similarly, Yuan
(2025) reported that Chinese EFL learners’ reading comprehension
augmented, their anxiety reduced using Smart Sparrow, an AI-driven reading
platform.
          Studies also reveal that AI positively influences learners’ emotional
factors, such as motivation, engagement, and anxiety, because AI supports
personalized and adaptive learning experiences, which are essential for
addressing diverse learner needs (e.g., Özçelik, 2025). For example, learners
can use conversational AI tools and practice their language skills more
confidently and autonomously in an interactive and low-anxiety self-paced
learning environment (Ekizer, 2025; Lai & Lee, 2024).
          AI offers significant benefits not only for learners but also for
teachers. AI can reduce educators’ workload through automated assessment,
grading, insights on learner progress and feedback (Abrar et al., 2025), helping
teachers manage their classrooms more efficiently (Luckin & Cukurova, 2019;
Szabó & Szoke, 2024). It can also aid in creating individualized instruction,
providing immediate feedback, and supporting self-regulated learning by
allowing learners to monitor and adjust their performance and progress
(Crompton et al., 2024). Furthermore, instructors have more time for
providing emotional support, developing cognitive abilities, communication
and interaction when AI does routine tasks (Yadav et al, 2025).
          On the other hand, research also underscores several challenges
associated with AI integration in ELT. Some notable challenges include
concerns of over-reliance on AI tools, potential reduction in critical thinking
and authentic interaction, and ethical concerns such as plagiarism and
academic integrity. Technological limitations and the lack of educational
programs or professional training for educators to effectively incorporate AI
into their teaching (Sahdrina et al., 2024) are also critical issues. Ramakrishnan
et al. (2024) argued that the effectiveness of AI integration into education may
depend on the instructors’ AI skills and knowledge.
          Another concern from a Global Englishes perspective is that AI
systems still may have accent bias as the tools prioritize native speakers’

accents (Kang & Hirschi, 2025). This can be attributed to the fact that AI
models are largely trained on English-language datasets originating from
Western academic and business environments, leading them to reinforce
standardized and Anglocentric language norms. Thus, excessive dependence
on AI-generated suggestions may constrain the creativity and adaptive
negotiation processes that are fundamental to human ELF communication
(Rudik & Ter-Grygoryan 2025). Moreover, a significant drawback is AI’s
inability to detect cultural sensitivity (Rudik & Ter-Grygoryan 2025), learners’
real emotions, motivation, body language, and facial expressions, which are
the crucial elements human teachers can monitor (Holmes et al., 2019). This
indicates that AI cannot replace teachers but can be a complementary tool
for more efficient classroom management.
         A recent systematic review on the use of AI in English language
teaching and learning by Crompton et al. (2024) identifies a great number of
affordances of AI in teaching and learning English as a global language. These
include personalized learning, self-regulated learning, learners’ reduced
anxiety, expanded vocabulary, enhanced writing skills, improved competence
in using the target language for communication, automatic marking,
providing feedback, adaptive educational experiences, intelligent tutoring and
prediction systems. However, the review also highlights critical challenges.
The first challenge is related to relevant published research which did not
report the challenges arising from the use of AI in the language classroom
due to the positive publication bias. The second challenge is related to the
standard language ideologies, which are in conflict with the Global Englishes
pedagogy. Thirdly, while research shows that AI helps to reduce learners’
anxiety, it is unknown whether AI can prepare learners to be anxiety-free
when facing with human interlocutors in their real-life conversations. Finally,
there has not been effective solutions to ethical challenges regarding ‘building
awareness about the limitations and risks of AI and debating the various
aspects of AI ethics’ (Ziesche & Kumar Bhagat, 2022).

                    AI Application in Thai ELT Context

         A rapid increase in research on AI technology in Thai ELT
demonstrates that many educational institutions in Thailand have started
implementing AI as a supporting tool in EFL classrooms (Raungsawat et al.,
2025). However, studies by Thai scholars (e.g. Chaipidech et al., 2022;
Ingkavara et al., 2022; Khampusaen, 2025; Limna & Saengchart, 2025;
Meniado et al., 2024; Pitukwong & Saraiwang, 2024; Tanharat & Phootirat,
2025; Thangthong et al., 2024) have shown that AI-oriented personalized
strategies enhance autonomy and teacher development in the context of Thai
higher education.

         Songsiengchai (2025) reported the results of their mixed-methods
study with 120 university Thai students divided equally into the control group
and experimental group. The aim of the study is to examine the effectiveness
of Artificial Intelligence (AI) models like Chat GPT to facilitate English
language learning. Quantitative data showed a statistically significant
difference in the learner outcome as measured in standardised English tests
between the two groups. Qualitative data collected from focus group
interviews demonstrated high motivation, strong self-confidence, and a
positive attitude shift among the students. While the findings of this study are
interesting, it is not clear about the benefits of AI to student individuals, and
the focus group interviews did not allow the diverse voices to be heard.
Particularly, there is no information reported regarding the tasks and the
materials used for learning driven by Chat GPT. Also, the study did not report
the challenges of using AI in teaching and learning, posing the problem of
positive publication bias.
         Apart from their impact on academic achievement, AI tools facilitate
individualized learning and increase learners' engagement (Kalra et al., 2026).
Learners gain linguistic confidence and motivation when they use AI tools,
as these tools improve the quality of their work through real-time feedback
and personalized guidance (Thangthong et al. 2024; Waluyo & Kusumastuti,
2024). Moreover, using AI tools before class acts as a valuable preparation
aid that helps students feel more confident, less anxious, and better prepared
to participate in lessons (Boontong et al. 2025). In addition, Thongsan and
Anderson (2025) found that learners showed awareness of bias in AI-
generated content and raised evaluative questions when interacting with AI.
This suggests that systematic integration of AI into pedagogy can also be
useful in fostering learners’ critical thinking and learner autonomy.
         In general, studies reveal the increased use of AI in ELT and its
significant pedagogical potential across various language skills. As educators
have begun using GenAI, they show positive attitudes toward AI, recognizing
its usefulness in daily routines such as writing tasks and generating ideas for
high-level academic work (Kohnke & Ulla, 2024). However, they also worry
about ethical concerns (Ulla et al., 2023), over-reliance on AI tools, which
may hinder in-depth learning and critical thinking (Limna & Saengchart,
2025) and reduce spontaneous interactions with lecturers (Boontong et al.
2025). Learners also express ethical concerns, including plagiarism
(Apridayani et al., 2025), information reliability (Tanharat & Phootirat, 2025),
and potential reduction in creativity (Apridayani et al., 2025). Taken together,
these opportunities and challenges suggest that educators must adapt their
role as AI becomes increasingly integrated into language education. The
educator’s role should shift from a provider of information to a guardian of
the learning experience, prioritizing human qualities that technology cannot

reliably replicate and guiding learners in the effective, ethical, critical use of
AI tools (Montakantiwong, A., & Jitpaisarnwattana, 2026).
         Waluyo and Kusumastuti (2024) used a mixed-methods approach to
explore the perspectives on the use of AI in their teaching and learning of the
students and teachers working in an English Department of a Thai university.
The authors reported that the students showed positive attitudes towards AI
tools. However, they also voiced their concerns about the overreliance of AI-
generated content. From teacher perspectives, the study reported teachers
were concerned about the challenges in using AI to access students’ learning
progress in such a way that can promote independent learning as well as
ethical issues such as academic integrity. The authors also recommend that
AI tools should be integrated into the current curriculum in ways that
complement traditional teaching methods. Similarly, Kalra et al. (2026)
examined the impact of AI on Thai university teachers’ teaching
methodologies and learners’ learning experiences. The analysis of data
collected via semi-structured interviews and focus group showed positive
results of the AI impact on student engagement, and their academic
performance. Yet, the authors emphasized the need of balanced
methodologies between AI-based pedagogies and traditional pedagogical
practices in Thai universities.
         Also, by using mixed-methods approach, Pinweha and Sapsirin (2026)
examined the vocabulary size of Thai graduate students and their perceptions
of how vocabulary knowledge influenced their use of AI in English language
learning. The results were mixed with some students expressing positive
views of AI on the growth of their vocabulary size, other suggesting no AI-
supported effect on their vocabulary size. The limitation of this study lies in
the reliance of students’ self-reports via interviews.
         Thadphoothon and Samrit (2025) conducted a classroom research
study using questionnaires to explore Thai university students’ use of AI to
learn English vocabulary. The authors reported students’ positive attitudes
towards the use of AI in learning new words and practicing pronunciation,
but the authors did not provide information about what pronunciation
models were chosen and who decided which models were considered
desirable or acceptable. Also, the study reported concerns about its reliability
and the need for supplementary traditional learning methods.
         Although the body of research on AI in ELT in Thai contexts is
remarkably growing, comprehensive evaluations of scalability remain limited.
The studies reported tensions in the use of AI for the purpose of improve
learning outcomes and teachers and students’ attitudes towards AI use.
Methodologically, most of studies used qualitative methods such as interviews
and focus group to collect the data whereas experimental studies tended to
be conducted by the classroom teachers themselves. It is not clear how the

intervention was designed, and implemented, how confounding variables
were controlled as most of these experiments were conducted in contact
groups. One critical issue is that the impact of AI use on learners’ learning
outcomes as reported in the studies, this impact may be credited to the
novelty effect. Without sufficient evidence of the long-term effects of AI-
assisted learning on language skills, it is challenging to validate the
effectiveness of these tools. The studies that employed a mixed-methods
approach is still limited in number.
        While some studies recommended that a balance between AI-based
pedagogy and tradition teaching methodologies should be considered, the
issue of how to integrate AI tools in traditional, human-centric teaching
methodologies is still ignored. Despite this weakness, research on the use of
AI in ELT in Thai educational contexts is of interest to researchers in other
Southeast Asian countries.

                               Recommendations

       The use of AI in ELT and research on its impact on learning outcome
in Thailand are still in their early stages. The journey toward a mature and
effective AI-enhanced ELT paradigm in Thailand demands a priority in
developing a sound pedagogy that balances the traditional teaching and
learning strategies with AI-supported teaching and learning strategies. By
following this forward-looking research agenda, the Thai ELT community
can move decisively beyond the current "technology as add on" or
“technology as fashion” phenomenon toward a local sustainable AI-
supported ELT pedagogy that is both innovative and culture-fit. For instance,
when utilizing an AI chatbot to generate dialogue or correspondence, a
teacher might design a collaborative activity where students critically analyze
the AI's output for Western biases or inappropriate tones. The teacher can
then guide the students in revising the text to reflect Thai cultural values, such
as appropriate levels of politeness and respect for elders, thereby acting as a
guardian of the learning experience. Additionally, the teacher could assign an
AI writing assistant to provide immediate, routine feedback on students'
grammatical errors. The teacher can then utilize the time saved from manual
grading to conduct personalized, face-to-face coaching sessions, offering the
emotional support, encouragement, and human interaction that AI cannot
replicate. This ensures that the deeply respected, traditional role of the teacher
as a mentor is preserved rather than replaced.
       This forward-looking journey requires an awareness of the potential
benefits of AI tools as well as a careful navigation of the inherent and situated
challenges with a view to ensuring that AI tools are effectively integrated into
the educational landscape. Such a journey must be supported with more

robust studies that focus on long-term effect of AI tools upon the teaching
and learning of English as a global language in Thailand. Such studies should
move beyond questionnaire- or interview-based surveys towards the adoption
of a mixed-methods approach. Studies on how AI tools are used to
complement and enhance the current curriculum rather than contradict or
complicate it should be encouraged. In the same vein, studies on how teachers
can find a middle ground between AI-based pedagogy and traditional
teaching methods to preserve the teacher-student relationship, which is
deeply rooted in Thai culture and other Asian cultures will be of great value.

                                       Conclusion

        As Cogo et al., (2024) have noted,

              The pace of advancement in GenAI has been absolutely
              incredible. It could be argued that this exacerbates a tension
              which has always existed to some extent: that between the
              typical speed of academic output versus the typical speed of
              technological developments. As educators, we may well want
              to include technology in our classroom practice, but we also
              want this practice to be judicious, to be informed by research
              and reflection, and these things take time. In the case of
              GenAI, it seems the gap in the time it takes for the tech to
              advance and the time it takes for us to study it and share our
              learnings has become wider than ever.
                                               (Cogo et al., 2024, p. 373-374)

         AI has now been integral to human life and is transforming all spheres
of human life including education. In ELT, AI offers both affordances and
challenges. As a result, ethical and pedagogical cautions must be taken to
approach the integration of AI in ELT. This is because research on the effect
of generative AI tools on education in Thai educational contexts and beyond
is still in its early stages and language instructors are still ‘finding their footing’.
In both global and Thai ELT contexts, AI is perceived as an advantageous
supplementary tool, specifically useful in developing EFL learners’ language
abilities and affective factors such as motivation and engagement. It can also
benefit EFL instructors in several ways, providing more chances to focus on
high-impact tasks while allowing AI to do the repetitive ones. Despite the
benefits, AI still has limitations, including the lack of AI policies and
structured ethical guidelines, so that its use with greater integrity can
encourage ethical and responsible practices. If it is widely used and users are
either formally or informally trained, the benefits might outweigh the
drawbacks in our society. In other words, AI in education in general and in
ELT in particular should not be viewed simply from the technological
LEARN Journal: Vol. 19, No. 2 (2026)                                               Page 10

Tangkiengsirisin et al. (2026), pp. 1-17
functionality perspectives but emphasis should be placed on the values,
intentions, and consequences that underpin its use. As a practical
contribution, future research must prioritize longitudinal, mixed-methods
studies to evaluate the long-term effectiveness of AI tools beyond initial
novelty effects. Furthermore, scholarly efforts should focus on designing
balanced pedagogies that harmoniously integrate AI with the human-centric,
traditional teacher-student relationships that are fundamental to Thai culture.

                                About the Authors

Supong Tangkiengsirisin: An associate professor at the Language Institute,
Thammasat University, with a PhD in English Studies from the University of
Nottingham, U.K. He is a former president of Thailand TESOL Association
with specialization in English language teaching and training. His research
interests include Second Language Writing, Written Discourse Analysis,
Global Englishes, and English for Specific/Academic Purposes.

Le Van Canh: A Professor of Applied Linguistics at Vietnam National
University, Hanoi, and a visiting professor at the Industrial University of Ho
Chi Minh City, where he lectures at the graduate levels. Also, he has been
invited as a guest lecturer by the Language Institute of Thammasat University,
Thailand twice (2024, 2025). His most recent publications appear in
Handbook of Research on Teacher Education (2022, published by Springer),
The Oxford Handbook of Southeast Asian Englishes (2024, published by
Oxford University Press) and The Routledge Handbook of Language
Teacher Education Research (2025, published by Routledge).

Sethawut Techasan: A full-time lecturer at Theodore Maria School of Arts,
Assumption University. He is an active committee member of Thailand
Extensive Reading Association (TERA). His research interests include
materials development, English for Specific Purposes, linguistics, and Global
Englishes.
